lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. Elections 2025. I would like to make some comments about the elections, comments not from a political point of view, but rather observations and personal thought I'd like to speak as an everyday ordinary person. I think we all had enough of the election since being swamped these last couple of months of news stories, election debates, people at our doors, and general conversations with like-minded people and those of another ilk. I have jotted down some personal thoughts and observations. On the provincial level, we had a leadership race for the Conservative Party of Manitoba. These 2 candidates, the race was between Abhi Khan and Wally Dawdridge, a race I think most people thought was closer than first expected. I think the actual percentages were 49.5 to 50.4 in favour of Mr. Khan. The question to be answered now is, can Abhi Khan pull the party together so it is not polarized such as the final count may indicate? Reading the headlines as of late, it appears that Dodridge wishes to remain as a party faithful, helping to unite its members. So my hat goes off to Abhi Khan for winning and to Wally Khan for his commitment to, to the cause. Khan, upon taking the helm of the party, immediately apologized for the party not doing more to facilitate the landfill project and ultimately recovering the remains of the 2 murdered Indigenous women. On the federal level, we saw turbulence starting 6 months ago that culminated on Election Day as a minority government was elected for the Liberals. During the election period, I took the opportunity to do some door knocking, as did other members as well. I was doing some door knocking for MP Ed Falk in Provincie and for former MP Marty Marantz in Winnipeg, representing the riding of Charleswood-St. James-The Assiniboine-Headingley. Since 2019. The results were that Falk won by a landslide and Morantz was narrowly defeated by the Liberals. When door knocking, and the response I received from people confirmed my assumption and beliefs that the Canadian electorate is fickle. This was a conclusion reached in both the urban and the rural areas. Numerous people I spoke to a couple of days before the election Assured me that they would be doing their due diligence over the weekend and researching both the Conservative and the Liberal parties. Most were concerned that crime was a major election priority, and they were unaware which party would be the toughest on crime. My thoughts and responses were, did we not now just complete 10 years of catch and release? The question left unanswered was where these individuals gravitate to in order to glean and seek their information from the internet, from CBC, from friends woven with similar cloth. Of all the people I spoke to, no one said they were supporting the NDP. These past 10 years of catch and release have definitely made it more difficult for the police, made more work for prosecutors and judges, and foremost, causing the general public to be less safe and more at risk for property damage and serious violent crime. Thank you. One lady I spoke to responded that her family had always voted Conservative but now cast their early vote for the Liberals. She said she was looking forward to a more comprehensive bail reform and tougher stance on crime. Again, I'm reminded that our past government had 10 years to enact such a law and to bring in reform. During all this time, the thought or opinion that I was left with was overarching attitude of people not committed to policies and positioning of their party, the party they supported, and what they— what the party stands for. I'm left concerned that people's convictions are fluid at election time, most often voting against a candidate or a party opposed to voting for someone, thus not weighing the platform or policies of the parties. Many, of course, have a mindset of what it is that their mindset is, what's in it for me? At the end of the day, I left confused and puzzled as I encouraged everyone of the importance of getting out to vote and every vote counts. Thank you, Mr. Mayor.

The purpose of the variance, V-2025-07, is twofold. First of all, to allow an overall site width of 64.5 feet, whereas a minimum site width of 75 feet is required in the RMD residential medium density zone. Secondly, to permit a corner side yard setback of 4 feet, whereas the RMD zone requires a minimum corner side yard setback of 8 feet. Notices as are required under the Planning Act have been issued. Other than correspondence from community planning, there is no other correspondence on file, and the comments from community planning indicates that it generally has no concerns with these rezoning application. As far as comments from administration, this existing property does contain a single-family residence. It is located at the Thank you. And as far as the proposal itself, the proposed access to the subject property would appear to have an appropriate setback from the intersection, and it would not appear that the requested site width reduction would have a negative impact on the proposed development or on the abutting roadways. The proposed site plan also shows that the project is able to be developed with Without the approval of the reduced corner side yard from the required 8 feet. Therefore, recommendation from administration is that council approve the application to vary the site width to permit a site of 64.5 feet where a minimum of 75 feet are required. However, to deny the application to vary the corner side yard setback to permit 4 feet where a minimum of 8 feet are required. Thank you. Further, with respect to the rezoning, the applicant does propose to develop a 6-unit residential structure on the site. The subject property, as I mentioned, is located at the corner of Loewen Boulevard and Henry Street. Thank you. lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. A couple of comments. Well, I think this is— first off, as you said, this is the first time that we've hired a consultant to develop any kind of a plan, active transportation plan for the city. lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: So I've appreciated the work that's gone into it and a lot of the recommendations that go around it. Thank you. And the history provided in this report has also been very good. And things that we have accomplished to date, we do have some great pathways. And if you spent any time at all on our pathways in Steinbach, whether it's Bush Farm or the path to the pool or the Clear Spring Greens or through the soccer park on Ellie Barkman Park, we do have a good pathway system that started. And now with the new development that Lang Hill Farms. Now the developers are starting to understand that, that how important pathways and active transportation is too. But this is also a little bit bigger than that. How do we move people outside of a vehicle? Our planning has always been in our community, like many communities, is how do we move the vehicles? It's not how do we move people outside of vehicles. So This is a good plan, and it also hinders some of the planning in our downtown core because our streets are set. And, uh, but I appreciate the information. I appreciate the information. There was a little bit of information on street calming. I appreciated that. I would have liked to see more on that. I also appreciated the Share the Road program, that you've moved it off of Loewen Boulevard and into other side streets, more the residential streets. So that makes That makes perfect sense. So that is something that I could see us doing, and that is a low-cost improvement, and I appreciate that recommendation. So ongoing, it's our older parts of the city, our core, that's always a struggle, but where we would have to— that's where the Share the Road program is a big piece of. I also see where we need to push more pedestrian traffic to our shopping centres, so we The recommendation is a sidewalk or a multi-use path on the west side, or on the west side of number 12, which is important. Today we cannot get to Superstore by walking or by bike without crossing private property or sharing the road, the very tight road, with vehicle traffic. So I think that is critical. Looping pathways is also important, that this would help with that. One of the problems I have Or one of the issues I see, and it was mentioned, is how do we cross some of our major streets and highways. But those are all choices that we'll have to make when we get to that point with the recommendations. There's a lot of information to absorb here, and I may have missed a few items listed, as I've read through it a number of times, and then now we hear presentation, there's new things that have come up. But this is a great first step in developing and being part of our long-term strategy. The pathway system developed by Lang Hill Farms Development is a great example of how incorporating active transportation into our developments will serve our residents well into the future. So future developments, then I would expect them to, to see that as well. But once accepted, this plan will be part of future planning, and as stated earlier, it's a good first step in developing a long-term strategy regarding our active transportation.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you. Anything further?

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. I will try not to echo the sentiments of Thank you, Councillor Siemens, although he covered a lot there. This is a great beginning step, and the City of Steinbach doesn't have— didn't have an active transportation, at least not a formal active transportation adopted, which often left us as council scratching our heads and saying, well, could we connect this and could we connect that? And the reality is we're not the professionals, and that's why we brought the consultants on board, because they came up with ideas that we didn't even think were necessarily on the table. One thing I do really appreciate is the look Thank you. I really appreciate the vision for the future. A lot of these projects are long-term, but they're long-term with purpose. If you look at the further— at the bigger map, you can see that there's kind of tendrils of active transportation that go into every area of Steinbach potentially in the future. And what that does is that gives the city the opportunity to, as development occurs on the peripheral areas, to get areas set aside already for active transportation. Another thing I really appreciate is that the future proposed paths are mostly off-road. We— unfortunately, there's only so much you can do with aged infrastructure. So in part of this plan, there is some shared pathway with regards to on the street. But ideally, as is reflected in the long-term plan here, it is to have multi-use paths that are off of streets. It's safer for pedestrians. It's better for automotive transportation as well. So it's a good plan. A lot of this probably won't even be enacted by Anybody that's on this council right now, but it's a good planning, a good long-term plan and some short-term solutions as well. So a good mix of everything to look at future active transportation.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you. Any further? Go ahead.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. I will support the motion as well. I think it's helpful to have a document that gives us a big picture look at active transportation within the city, and that's certainly what this does for it. I look at this as Thank you. I think of this as a general— you can think of it as a general plan that in principle these are some of the things that we will look at and consider in the future. I certainly do like the idea of having more pathways, and this has identified, you know, some possibilities. The price tags are very high, and so no one should look at this and assume that, okay, all of this is going to happen in the near term. As the document itself says, much of this is significantly in the future. When you add this all together, I think it added up to $11 million in total. That won't be happening anytime soon. But as far as doing some of the things in here, especially some of the shared— share the road, some of that additional signage, that certainly is reasonable and that could be done in the shorter term. One thing that's important to me is to make sure that any planning that we do with active transportation does not hinder or get in the way of vehicle transportation. People do drive cars, and I have no intention of Preventing people from doing that or telling people they shouldn't be driving their cars. We want to obviously facilitate for anyone who wants to walk and ride a bicycle, that is great. The reality is that most people in Steinbach do drive vehicles, particularly in the winter months, and we're not going to do anything to impede that. Also, in terms of some of the details in here, not everything in here is something that I am looking at wanting to do. I think it's For example, you know, when you look at the sidewalk section, some of the sidewalks that are listed here that are proposed are on streets that are very well established, and that what we found in the past is that when you start trying to put sidewalks into very established neighbourhoods, you tend to get a lot of neighbourhood opposition because of the impact it has on driveways, trees, shrubs, and that. Back in 2007, for example, because Madison Drive is one of the ones that's mentioned here as a proposed sidewalk, Yes. The city had planned to put a sidewalk along there, and there was overwhelming opposition on Madison Drive, and we removed it. That was one of the very first things that happened when— after Councillor Siemens and I were elected to council, was we dealt with massive neighborhood opposition there. And so it's important to keep that in mind as well. But again, this plan is not saying that we're going to do all of this. It's saying here's a big picture look at here are some of the things that we can do in the future, and I think the document is helpful. So I certainly am in favour of accepting it and using it in our future planning process.

lines.text: Thank you. Anything further, council? Anything closing?

lines.text: Just to echo Councillor Zwaagstra, that I do remember Madison Drive and I do remember the feedback. lines.text: Well, council, it's kind of really neat that this Saturday at the Picketman Walk, a small group of youth cornered me and they wanted to talk about Exactly this. And that's where this is. You know, council, we've tried our best. On the 15 years I've been on council, we've approved many sidewalk plans, many Pathway plans, and I think we've done a good job without having a plan. What I think this is good about this is we will have a plan. There'll be a targeted— not that we're going to do everything every year, but we're going to do some things every year, and we're going to have a targeted plan so that after a certain amount of time, we will have this done, and then we'll need a new plan. And I think that's what's exciting is that now We have something to work on. Little by little, we'll whittle away at it and we'll get it done, and we will enhance our neighborhoods, and we will enhance our family times with— inside of families. They'll be able to do— because not everyone wants to ride bikes. Some like to longboard and some like to scooter, and we see that all the time on our pathways that are close to our house. And so for that reason, I'm actually very glad to see this, and I think this is a step in the right direction. Again, it was said before, this is a first step. And, but this is, I do believe this is better than what we've been doing. And I mean, the last, I think one of the last regional pathways we did was when we had a neighborhood, a community came to us and asked, And asked for a delegation and asked for a path, and then we worked on it. That worked in that situation, but in this situation, I think it's going to work way better to be proactive instead of reactive. Call for the question. All those in favor? Opposed? That is carried. lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. Just something I want to bring up to council and just ask a general question. As council knows, Mayor Funk and I are on the, the RCMP Advisory Committee where we meet regularly with a couple community members and our acting detachment commander, Joanne Ryle. We obviously— traffic enforcement is important in our city, and we have certainly in the last couple months have heard more reports from people noticing racing on Main Street and, and, and obviously desiring more enforcement. And so at our most recent advisory meeting, we had encouraged our staff sergeant or sergeant to look at any options in terms of getting more enforcement. The reality is, is that like many other cities across the country, Uh, we don't have our full RCMP complement, as the RCMP is not— has not been able to get the full numbers that we're— that we've requested. We're often 2, 3, or 4 officers short of the amount that we have requested, and of course that affects the ability to do proper enforcement. And so one of the, uh, one of the proposals that Sergeant Ryle had made is those working together with the Town of Ste. Anne to do some collaborative enforcement, and this has been reported in the media lately. Thank you. That there have been some— that there's been some joint enforcement of traffic along Main Street between both the— between our local RCMP and Ste. Anne. And the request was made that from Ste. Anne, a proposal that they're willing to do some additional enforcement that they would do more independently, and they would do it through funding provided by Manitoba Public Insurance. This is money that's provided to police forces to do extra traffic enforcement, often using overtime for officers. So it's not taking away from regular policing duties, but it's using extra hours. And so the request simply is, are we okay with having additional traffic enforcement in the city, continuing with the cooperation with Ste. Anne, and then also allowing for a certain number of hours each week With Ste. Anne doing some extra enforcement. And the way that I would look at it, and the feedback we'd gotten from the advisory committee as a whole, is that this is an important issue, particularly when you've got the issues such as the racing on Main Street. This is something that— which is obviously very unsafe, and it's a major noise issue, and people want to see more enforcement. And I'm open to a— You know, I think we got to do whatever we can to to catch these individuals. And frankly, if you don't like the fact you're getting pulled over by a Ste. Anne officer while you're racing down Main Street, I don't care, because you shouldn't be racing down Main Street. So if your car gets impounded, I don't really care which officer it is that's impounding your car. Tough luck. But the question I just want to ask is, is council okay with this proposal for, for some of this, for some additional enforcement?

lines.speaker: Earl Funk

lines.text: Yes, council, this is The question's before us, is there consensus for something like this to go on? I do want to say this is nothing new. They do cell phones and they do do speeding and traffic violations. So this is quite common. The one good thing is the 2 police forces working together in cooperation to make a safer— a safety— a more safe southeast area. And so, but council, it looks like we've got consensus for this. Thank you. You're okay? And so then we'll— we will then— I guess we'll have Mr. Warkentin, you'll reach out to Joanne and let her know that council was okay with this?

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: The cost of running a library, as Many things has gone up substantially, especially since COVID and it is in May 2023 when COVID was officially over. That's only 2 years ago. The 2 largest areas of cost is wages and cost of books. Both have had substantial increases. Our wages, including this October's upcoming October's minimum wage increase, that means our, our minimum wages have increased close to 40%, and our book purchases have increased 60% plus, and right now it is unknown what the new tariffs could potentially impact future book purchases. So there is a large concern with the amount of books that we can purchase. Recently, the library board made a presentation to city council regarding the many issues facing the library, and part of the discussion was various fees the library charges. Excuse me. And one— and council asked the library board if they could review their non-resident fees, which they did. Similar to other city facilities, the pool or the arena, roughly 35 to 40% of the library users are non-residents, and we need to increase those fees to the level similar to what our residents pay. It's, it's simply that simple, and our residents pay through their property taxes. Non-resident fees are not only the Are not the only fees that are being increased, as many of the service and room rental fees have also been adjusted. It should be noted that the frontline library staff that deal with the users and will have to deal with the heat will be the ones that will need to answer all the different questions. Bringing this to council's attention and then that way through the public will also help reduce the negative feedback that the staff feel that they're going to be committed to. But at this point, it is important that that in order to meet budget obligations and potentially open up the library to full hours again, we do need to raise our revenues. That wasn't tears of joy. Anyways, I just want council to be aware of that, and no particular thing, but I needed— felt I needed to speak to it so that It became part of public record.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: I'm just wondering if there was anything you can update on regionalization.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: Excuse me. Yes, thank you, Mr. Mayor. There's another committee that I've been assigned to, and that's the Regional Library Committee for Southeastern Manitoba. Councillor Bill Hiebert and myself have been assigned to that. To date, 8 municipalities continue to take part of those discussions. The Public Library Services Board is chairing the meetings and much information is shared. The last regional meeting— well, the last regional library that was formed in Manitoba was in 2002. Only Eastman doesn't have a regional library besides the small one that is between St. Pierre and the Arm of the Salisbury in St. Mauro. Our next meeting is May 22nd. And it will be an in-person meeting in Niverville, and it will include leadership from the Interlake and the South Central Library Boards so that we can begin discussions on what does regionalization look like, what are the costs, what are the benefits that the RMs are getting, the communities are getting, and how does it— how do you put it together? There's a lot of heavy lifting that has to happen if this is in fact is going to take place. The process is not a quick one. If in fact that we do regionalize, and this is a positive and it does happen, the earliest, absolute earliest, this would be with 2027. Simply, there is too much to do. And it is my opinion, and likely of this council and other councils, it comes down to 2 things: what are— what's going to be the cost and what services do we get for those costs? And we can't answer those 2 things until we put a framework together and understand what every community needs and/or municipality needs, but every municipality has a different need because there is French services, there are libraries in schools, there's libraries that are only open one day a week. There's such a variety of things that have to be worked through, so there's a lot of heavy lifting that has to be done to To get it manageable. Besides the May 22nd meeting, we have a meeting on June 5th, which then completes the 4 initial meetings that we had committed to as a council. A further review meeting will be called in September where all interested municipalities are then asked to attend, and at that point there's going to be a decision made whether there's a commitment from all the municipalities to continue moving forward. And I keep asking the question, what's the vision? Thank you. And so the vision is to have one regional library for all of southeastern Manitoba, similar to what's in all the Interlakes, similar to what's in the Parkland region, and similar to what's in the South Central. So that is overriding vision, but there's a lot of work to be done in order to get it there. So I appreciated the comments from Councillor Hiebert at the meetings as well because— I agree. Those are long meetings and there's lots of opinions being shared by a variety of municipalities. So we're working on that too, Mr. Mayor.
